questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit review the TTAB’s legal conclusions de novo but factual findings for substantial evidence?
questions.question_body: The opinion says “We review the Board’s legal conclusions de novo, and its findings of fact for substantial evidence.” I’m confused about the distinction. When does an appellate court apply de novo review to a TTAB decision, and what exactly qualifies as a “finding of fact” that gets the substantial‑evidence standard? Also, how does this affect the weight given to the Board’s analysis of the DuPont factors?

questions.title: What is the proper scope of the sixth DuPont factor when the parties’ services are found to be highly similar?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board’s analysis of the sixth factor because it limited the “relevant public” to credit‑card consumers and ignored other Aspire marks used for banking/financing services. Should the sixth factor always consider all similar marks on any similar goods, even if the goods aren’t identical? How does the earlier finding on the second factor (goods similarity) constrain the analysis of the sixth factor?

questions.title: How does the removal of “credit card services” from the USPTO ID Manual affect the likelihood‑of‑confusion analysis?
questions.question_body: The Board noted that the ID Manual no longer lists “credit card services” and therefore defined the term itself. Does the absence of a term from the manual make a difference in interpreting a filing’s description of services, or is the Board free to adopt its own definition? How binding is the ID Manual in this context?

questions.title: When can the TTAB ignore third‑party marks that are not on the identical goods in the sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: In this case, the Board treated only Aspire marks used for credit‑card services as relevant and dismissed the other 42 marks used for broader financial services. Is there precedent allowing the Board to narrow the universe of comparable marks, or must it consider any similar mark on any similar service once the underlying goods are deemed “highly similar”?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the first DuPont factor analysis along with the sixth factor?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the first factor must be reconsidered because the sixth factor’s remand could change the commercial impression of the marks. How does the analysis of the number and nature of similar marks (sixth factor) influence the overall commercial impression (first factor)? Is this a common practice to vacate multiple factors together?

questions.title: What standard does the court apply to determine whether services are “legally identical, in part” under the second DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: The Board concluded that banking/finance services “legally” include issuing credit cards, and the appellate court affirmed that finding. What legal authority or test governs this “legal identity” analysis, and how does it differ from a purely factual similarity assessment?

questions.title: How does the Federal Circuit treat a TTAB’s failure to consider a “considerable” number of similar marks under the sixth factor?
questions.question_body: The opinion references cases like Jack Wolfskin and Juice Generation on what counts as “considerable” evidence of third‑party use. What quantitative or qualitative threshold must be met for the Board’s analysis to be deemed sufficient, and what happens if the Board’s sample is deemed too limited?

questions.title: What procedural steps must the TTAB take on remand after a Federal Circuit vacates its findings on the first and sixth DuPont factors?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board’s findings and remanded for reconsideration. Does the TTAB have to redo the entire likelihood‑of‑confusion analysis from scratch, or can it rely on its prior factual findings (e.g., the second factor) and only re‑evaluate the vacated factors? What is the standard of review on this second round of appeal?
